title: Addressing oral health inequalities: Why a life-course approach matters
html:
Fraser Macdonald, Dental Tribune International

Thu. 26. November 2026

share save

LONDON, England: Although the socio-economic causes of oral health inequalities are well known, interventions tend to focus on oral health education and individual behaviour change. A recent review has examined how a life-course perspective can be integrated with established public health strategies to inform oral disease prevention and policy. Using caries as an example, the authors illustrate how preventive action can be coordinated across different life stages and at individual, community and population levels.

Dr Richard Holmes, co-author of the study and senior lecturer in dental public health at Newcastle University in the UK. (Image: Dr Richard Holmes)

A life-course approach considers how social, economic and environmental circumstances influence health from pregnancy and childhood to adolescence, adulthood and older age. Two important concepts underpin this approach: critical or sensitive periods, when particular exposures can have a greater influence on future health, and the accumulation of risk, whereby prolonged or repeated disadvantage contributes to poorer outcomes over time. The authors argue that focusing solely on individual behaviours, such as oral hygiene and dietary choices, overlooks the wider circumstances that shape people’s ability to maintain good oral health.

Building on this understanding of how risks develop and accumulate over time, the review examines how a life-course perspective can be integrated with two established public health strategies: the common risk factor approach and population-level prevention. The former addresses risk factors shared by oral and general diseases, while the latter focuses on the wider social and environmental conditions that influence health. The authors advocate combining individual preventive care with wider community and population-level interventions.

In illustrating a life-course approach to caries prevention, the authors outline measures at national and local levels, including sugar taxation, advertising restrictions and controls on fast food outlets near schools. They also identify healthcare interventions in settings other than primary care, such as school-based toothbrushing programmes and oral health support in residential care facilities. These examples illustrate how interventions beyond the dental practice can complement clinical prevention at different stages of life.

Speaking to Dental Tribune International on the significance of the review, co-author Dr Richard Holmes, senior lecturer in dental public health at Newcastle University in the UK, stated: “Dental professionals have a critical role to play in being advocates for patients across their life-course. A life-course perspective may help dental teams to optimise their integration of tools such as the common risk factor approach with other evidence-based disease prevention activities. Ultimately, we hope that dental professionals will continue to be strong advocates for greater oral health equity across the lifespan.”

For dental teams, the review emphasises continuity of care, signposting patients to wider support services and collaboration with other healthcare and social care professionals. The authors also suggest making fuller use of the diverse skills of the oral health workforce to support patients at different stages of life. The authors conclude that tackling oral health inequalities requires coordinated action across the lifespan, addressing not only individual risk factors but also the social, commercial and political conditions that influence health.

The study, titled “A life course approach to population oral health”, was published on 13 November 2026 in the British Dental Journal.
